1: Berlin dub techno with the mixing desk left switched on — one chord, tape hiss, delay, and almost nothing else. The starter culture: it announces nothing, it just makes the room darker and warmer.
2: The opening joke and also a genuinely great record — a Rhodes loop that never resolves, riding for nine minutes. Burnt, deep and French. The spice arrives politely.
3: Detroit's least tidy producer handed to Detroit's tidiest. Craig builds one enormous crescendo and refuses to release it — the best patience record either of you owns.
4: Yoruba spirituality routed through Frankfurt. Âme turn a percussion record into a slow-motion tension coil; the first real heat of the night.
5: The man who invented deep house, twenty years on, still playing jazz chords over a drum machine — and Mr. White singing like he means every word. Warm rye, no crust yet.
6: Durban to Berlin. Rolling Afro-house carrying the low end of a much harder record. First point where the floor stops being polite.
7: The Chandler kick, a shaker, and a bassline that goes under the floorboards. Deep house that behaves like techno — built for a big room and a long blend.
8: Decades of New York ballroom are built on this one horn stab. Pure percussion, no melody, guaranteed reaction. Pepper's calling card.
9: Made when Trent was eighteen and still the most hypnotic thing here: one riff, twelve minutes, and it gets more menacing the longer you leave it alone.
10: Carl Craig's jazz drums cut loose — the record every drum & bass producer names as the moment. Broken, hot, impossible to predict.
11: Basic Channel's dancefloor alias. A chord decaying into pure hiss over a kick you can lean your whole weight on. Peak loaf.
12: Paris by way of West Africa: congas, a bassline that walks, no chorus anywhere. Africanism-era house that moves a floor sideways rather than up.
13: Gqom from Durban — half-time, all bottom, drums arranged like a threat. Slower than everything around it and hits harder than all of it.
14: Bulgarian machine funk with a rubber acid line KiNK plays live like an instrument. The lift out of the house section and into the mill.
15: The darkest record Chicago ever pressed. A sampled voice, a 303 in a foul mood, and enough space between the drums to be frightening.
16: Armando's 303 as pure aggression — the Chicago answer to the idea that acid is friendly. Short, fast, and completely unhinged.
17: The machine being misused for the first time, at length. Play more of it than feels sensible; it is the origin story of half this set.
18: Frankfurt's contribution to the argument: three 303s stacked and slowly opened. German engineering applied to a squelch.
19: Acid, but sad — Vienna's Johannes Auvinen singing over the 303. Gives the section a heart before it turns brutal.
20: Dutch bedroom electro, tape-saturated, with a bassline like a boiler room. It has no business being this funky.
21: Detroit's aquatic mythology at full speed. Electro that swims, from the Aquatic Invasion EP — the point where the tempo stops asking permission.
22: Carl Craig with one loop and no mercy. This is the record that turns a house set into a techno set; everything after it is the bake.
23: The most effective four bars in Chicago history — one wobbling synth figure and a catchphrase the whole field shouts back. Ridiculous, unstoppable.
24: Berlin, 1993, and still the heaviest thing on the list. Almost no information at all: a kick, a hum, and a room.
25: Frankfurt's rudest export — a bassline engineered to hurt a PA, and one of the few 2000s techno records that still detonates a festival on sight.
26: "Is that still going?" Yes. A joke that became a monster: a rubber-band bassline that simply keeps climbing until the room gives up.
27: Cajmere's alter ego narrating a school tour of a rave. Absurd, sinister, and it has never once failed.
28: A soul vocal chopped into a stutter over drums like a factory floor. Self-released, sold out on sight, and still the record that defines heavy UK dance music of the 2010s.
29: Hamburg, hardware only, no computer anywhere. Electro with the treble turned up until it bites — the spiciest thing in the crust.
30: There is no version of this that does not work. The loop, the ride, and a field losing it. Do not overthink the mix; just let it arrive.
31: The modern one. A chopped vocal over breakbeat and enormous sub — built for exactly this hour of exactly this kind of night.
32: Ten minutes of one arpeggio getting brighter and brighter. Not subtle, and neither is a festival at 21:40.
33: New York, dark, deliberately wrong-footed. The record that lets you step down from full pace without losing anybody.
34: Underground Resistance's most beautiful record and the emotional top of the night. Strings over a UR kick — play it, then let the floor breathe.
35: Manuel Göttsching's guitar loop, made in Italy, remixed by Detroit — and Pepper's whole thesis in one record. Warm, endless, Latin, and it buys you twelve minutes.
36: Detroit's saddest chord progression. Nobody has improved on it in nearly thirty years of trying.
37: The disco sample everyone knows, cut into something wistful. Engineered for the moment the sun is long gone and everyone realises the night is finite.
38: Chic looped by a man who refuses to explain himself. Grown, warm and slightly drunk — a Detroit basement at four in the morning.
39: The oldest record here and the one that needs no explanation. Six notes, and the whole building sings the bassline.
40: Robert Hood as Floorplan: a gospel vocal over Detroit techno. Both hands on the mixer, both of you grinning. There is no better way to hand a floor back.
101: Chain Reaction at its most patient — the same Berlin logic as the opener, with more air around it. Swap in if the room arrives late.
102: Manchester's cheerful acid, for the night where the Grinder reads meaner than the floor you actually got.
103: Where Detroit techno starts. Colder and stranger than anything in the Crust — the lever if the peak needs a reset rather than more pressure.
104: Chicago 1988, the reply record — Armando dissing back over a Mike Dunn house mix. Reach for it if the Grinder is landing and the floor wants one more before the peak.
105: Minimal techno as Hood defined it, off the record that named the idea. Use it when Crust needs to get harder rather than hotter.
106: The other way to end: warm, melodic, and it makes people hug each other. Swap for anything in the Last Slice.
